CS001.problem: By 1900 mathematicians had grown confident that every theorem could be derived from a few self-evident starting points. Then paradoxes appeared in the foundations. Bertrand Russell’s, found in 1901, showed that the innocent-sounding idea of “the collection of all collections that do not contain themselves” contradicts itself. If the foundations could produce contradictions, everything built on them was suspect. Gottlob Frege had tried to derive arithmetic from pure logic, and Russell’s paradox seemed to wreck his system. Mathematics needed foundations it could trust, and a way to check that trust.
CS001.insight: Alfred North Whitehead and Russell rebuilt mathematics from the ground up in a fully symbolic language, where every step is written out and justified by an explicit rule rather than by intuition. To block the paradox they sorted everything into a hierarchy of “types”: a collection may only contain things of a lower type than itself, so nothing can contain itself. Then, over three volumes, they derived the properties of numbers and much else from logic alone. The lasting point was less any single proof than the demonstration that proof itself can be treated as the manipulation of symbols.
CS001.analogy: It is the difference between explaining a recipe in words and writing it so exactly that a robot with no sense of taste could follow it. Nothing is left to judgment; only the rules decide.
CS001.unlocked: Treating proof as mechanical symbol manipulation made a new kind of object available for study: the formal system. Gödel’s incompleteness theorems are about a system of exactly this kind, and Church and Turing’s definitions of computation grew from asking what it means to follow rules mechanically. McCulloch and Pitts borrowed its logical notation to describe neurons. In 1956 the Logic Theorist, an early AI program, proved theorems from Principia’s second chapter, and the ideal of fully explicit derivations is the distant ancestor of today’s proof assistants and automated reasoning tools.
CS001.left_open: The system was vast and clumsy: the proof that 1 + 1 = 2 arrives hundreds of pages in. Some of its axioms, such as the axiom of infinity, did not look purely logical. Above all, the hope that the system could settle every mathematical question was a promise, not a proven fact. Whether any such complete and trustworthy system could exist was exactly what Kurt Gödel would answer two decades later.

CS002.problem: David Hilbert had set mathematicians a goal: place mathematics on a permanently secure footing. The recipe was to write down a formal system like Principia’s and then prove, by simple finite reasoning, that it is consistent (it never proves a falsehood) and complete (every statement is either provable or refutable). Principia had supplied the kind of system; what remained was the proof that it behaved. Many expected this to be a matter of time and effort rather than a matter of principle.
CS002.insight: Gödel noticed that statements about formulas and proofs can be turned into statements about numbers, by giving every symbol, formula and proof a numeric code. This is now called Gödel numbering. Once a system can talk about numbers, it can indirectly talk about itself. He constructed a sentence which, once decoded, says “this sentence is not provable in this system.” If the system proves it, the system proves something false. If it does not, the sentence is true but unprovable. So any consistent system strong enough for arithmetic must contain true statements it cannot prove. His second theorem added that such a system cannot prove its own consistency.
CS002.analogy: It is a cousin of the liar paradox, “this statement is false,” with truth swapped for provability. That small change turns a paradox into a theorem: the system’s own machinery for certifying statements cannot certify this one.
CS002.unlocked: It ended Hilbert’s programme in its original form. For computing, its method mattered as much as its conclusion. Encoding programs, proofs and statements as data is exactly the move Turing and Church would make, and it is the same idea that lets one program read, run or analyse another. Gödel also used primitive recursive functions, an early precise class of calculable functions, which pointed toward a mathematical definition of computation. Verification and program analysis still live with its consequence: no fixed method can prove everything that is true.
CS002.left_open: Gödel’s theorems were about provability inside particular formal systems. They did not say what a “mechanical procedure” is in general; that notion was still informal. And a sharper question remained: even if we cannot prove everything, could some mechanical method at least decide which statements are provable? That was Hilbert’s Entscheidungsproblem, and it stayed open until 1936.

CS003.problem: After Gödel, the question shifted from “can everything be proved?” to “can we at least decide, mechanically, what is provable?” Answering it needed a precise definition of “mechanical procedure.” Without one, nobody could prove that no such procedure exists. Words like algorithm or effective calculation were intuitions, not definitions, and a proof of impossibility needs something exact to be impossible about. Mathematicians had many examples of calculations but no agreed boundary around the idea.
CS003.insight: Alonzo Church proposed that “effectively calculable” should mean what can be expressed in his lambda calculus, a tiny language in which everything is a function. It has just two moves: create a function, and apply a function to an argument. Numbers, arithmetic, logic and repetition can all be encoded as functions. With this definition he proved that some problems, such as deciding whether two lambda expressions are equivalent, cannot be solved by any calculation. He also showed that lambda-definable functions match Gödel and Herbrand’s general recursive functions, which suggested the definition captured something natural. The claim that this really is what “calculable” means is now called Church’s thesis.
CS003.analogy: Imagine building all of programming from a single move: write a recipe with a blank in it (“take x and do this to it”), then plug something into the blank. Counting, choosing and repeating are all made by plugging recipes into recipes.
CS003.unlocked: Church gave the first precise answer to “what is computation?” and the first example of a problem no computation can solve. His notation became the root of functional programming: LISP borrowed it directly, and its descendants (ML, Haskell, and the lambda expressions in modern Python, JavaScript and Java) carry it forward. It also gave programming-language theory a way to say what a program means, by treating computation as the step-by-step simplification of expressions, an idea that still underlies how languages are specified and compilers reason about code.
CS003.left_open: Many logicians were not convinced that function substitution captured everything a human calculator does. A language of nested substitution does not obviously resemble working through a calculation on paper. The definition needed independent support, and it arrived within months from Alan Turing, who started from a very different picture: a machine that reads and writes symbols on a tape.

CS004.problem: Church had a definition of effective calculation, but it felt arbitrary. Hilbert’s Entscheidungsproblem asked for a mechanical procedure that decides whether any statement of logic is provable. To show no such procedure exists, one needed a definition of “mechanical” so obviously right that nobody could argue the procedure had been defined too narrowly. What was missing was a picture of calculation that people would accept at a glance.
CS004.insight: Turing started from what a human calculator does: work on paper, look at one symbol at a time, keep a limited amount in mind, and write or change marks. Stripped to essentials, that is a tape divided into cells, a head that reads and writes one symbol at a time, and a finite table of rules. This is a Turing machine. He then made two leaps. First, a single “universal” machine can read the description of any other machine from its tape and imitate it, so one machine can perform every computation: programs are data. Second, a diagonal argument shows that no machine can decide, for every machine, a question closely related to whether it will ever stop. Hence the Entscheidungsproblem has no solution. Turing also showed his machines compute exactly what Church’s lambda calculus does.
CS004.analogy: A record player is one device that plays any record, because the music is on the disc, not in the machine. The universal machine is the same trick for computation: the “disc” is a description of what to compute.
CS004.unlocked: The paper fixed the meaning of “computable,” proved the first limits of computation, and in the universal machine foreshadowed the general-purpose computer, the stored program, interpreters and compilers. It gave later computer science its standard model: complexity theory counts steps of Turing machines, and Turing returned to the machine picture in 1950 to ask whether machines can think. That Church’s and Turing’s independent definitions turned out to agree is the main reason the Church–Turing thesis is trusted.
CS004.left_open: A Turing machine says what is computable in principle, not what is computable efficiently or in reasonable time. It is a mathematical idealisation with an endless tape, not a blueprint for building a machine. And the Church–Turing thesis can never be proved, because “effectively calculable” is an informal idea. Questions of cost, how many steps and how much memory, would need a new theory.

CS005.problem: Telephone exchanges and early automatic machines were built from thousands of relays, electromagnetic switches that are either open or closed. Engineers designed these circuits by intuition, sketches and trial and error. There was no systematic way to know that a circuit did what was intended, or whether a simpler one would do the same job. As networks of switches grew, design by hand became unmanageable. A single wiring mistake in such a tangle was hard to find, and every redundant switch cost money.
CS005.insight: Claude Shannon, then a master’s student at MIT, noticed that a switch has two states, just as a statement in George Boole’s algebra of logic is either true or false. Two switches in series let current through only if both are closed, which is AND. Two in parallel let current through if either is closed, which is OR. A contact that is closed when its relay is off acts as NOT. So any circuit can be written as a Boolean expression, simplified with algebra, and rebuilt in a cheaper form; and any logical statement can be wired up as a circuit that computes it.
CS005.analogy: Picture two doors in a corridor: to get through you need both open (AND). Picture two alternative corridors: you get through if either is open (OR). Shannon saw that the plumbing of switches and the algebra of logic are the same thing, so simplifying one simplifies the other.
CS005.unlocked: This is the foundation of digital circuit design. Logic gates, adders and control units follow from the correspondence, and so does the practice of minimising circuits by algebra. It tied abstract logic to physical machines: whether built from relays, vacuum tubes or transistors, a computer’s logic is Boolean. Designers of the first stored-program computers used this style of reasoning, and it remains the language in which chip designers describe hardware today.
CS005.left_open: The thesis treated circuits as pure logic, with the output fixed by the current inputs. It said little about memory, timing, or how to organise switches into a whole computer: that needed an architecture. And it said nothing yet about what travels through circuits. Shannon himself would take that up a decade later by asking how much information a signal carries.
CS005.diagram_alt: Two switches A and B in series on one wire (current flows only if both are closed, AND) and in parallel on two branches (current flows if either is closed, OR), with a key stating series is AND, parallel is OR and a normally closed contact is NOT.

CS006.problem: Brains are made of neurons that either fire or do not, yet thought seems limitless and abstract. In the early 1940s no one had a precise way to say how a network of simple cells could compute anything, let alone reason. Neuroscience and logic spoke separate languages, and it was unclear whether the mind could be explained by the first at all.
CS006.insight: Warren McCulloch, a neurophysiologist, and Walter Pitts, a young logician, proposed a deliberately simplified neuron. It receives signals from other neurons and fires only if enough excitatory inputs arrive and no inhibitory input blocks it. Wire several together and they behave like AND, OR and NOT gates. They argued that any logical expression can be realised by a suitably wired network, and that networks given a tape to read and write could compute anything a Turing machine can. On this picture the brain is a computing device, and the mind’s operations are logical ones. Concretely, a neuron that needs both of two inputs to fire computes AND, one that needs either computes OR, and one that an inhibitory signal can silence gives NOT.
CS006.analogy: A neuron is a committee that votes: it acts if enough members say yes and nobody uses a veto. Chain committees together and you can compute any yes-or-no decision.
CS006.unlocked: This was the first mathematical model of a neural network, and it started the line of work that leads through Rosenblatt’s perceptron to modern deep learning. It also made “the mind as computation” a research claim. John von Neumann borrowed the idealised neuron as the basic building block in his EDVAC design, and the Dartmouth proposal listed neuron nets among its research topics. The idea that simple units wired together can compute anything remains the premise of every neural network today.
CS006.left_open: The model neurons had fixed connections and thresholds, so the network could not learn. Real neurons are far messier than on-off switches. How a network might adjust its own connections from experience, which is what makes brains, and later machines, flexible, was left untouched. It would take Hebb’s ideas, the perceptron, and eventually backpropagation to address it.

CS007.problem: Early electronic computers such as ENIAC were fast, but programming them meant physically rewiring cables and setting switches, which could take days. Memory was scarce and expensive. As the Moore School team planned a successor, they needed a clean design for a general-purpose machine whose task could be changed quickly, and a way to describe that design without tying it to one kind of electronic component.
CS007.insight: John von Neumann’s report described a machine of a few functional parts: a central arithmetic unit, a central control unit, a memory, and input and output. The crucial choice was a single memory holding both the data and the instructions, all encoded as numbers. A program could then be loaded like data, changed while running, and executed from memory one instruction after another. The report also described the machine’s logic organs as idealised neurons in the style of McCulloch and Pitts, which let the design be reasoned about without committing to a particular electronic technology.
CS007.analogy: Imagine a kitchen where recipe cards and ingredients sit on the same shelves. The cook can fetch a card just as easily as a carrot, and can even rewrite a card in the middle of cooking. That shared shelf is the stored program.
CS007.unlocked: The “von Neumann architecture” is still how nearly every computer is organised. Because programs are data, software could be separate from hardware, which made assemblers, compilers and operating systems possible, and so an entire software industry. A machine that could be reprogrammed in minutes instead of days turned computers from special-purpose calculators into general tools, the practical counterpart of Turing’s universal machine. Within a few years, working stored-program machines such as the Manchester Baby (1948) and EDSAC in Cambridge (1949) proved the idea in practice.
CS007.left_open: A single path between processor and memory becomes a bottleneck, and the design is inherently sequential. The report was an unfinished draft, circulated under one name, and who deserved credit for the ideas was disputed. Most pressing for users, programs still had to be written as numeric machine instructions by hand, a laborious and error-prone task that motivated the first high-level languages.
CS007.diagram_alt: A control unit and an arithmetic unit connected to a single memory that holds both instructions and data as numbers, with input and output devices attached to the memory.

CS008.problem: Telephone, telegraph and radio engineers thought in terms of voltages, bandwidth and signal strength. There was no way to say how much information a message contains, or what the best possible rate of reliable communication over a noisy line is. Many believed that noise forced a bargain: the more reliable you wanted the message, the slower you had to send it, with perfect reliability costing infinite time.
CS008.insight: Claude Shannon defined information by surprise: the less likely a message, the more information it carries. Counted in bits, the average information of a source is its entropy, and the meaning of the message is irrelevant to the engineering problem. He then proved two surprising results. A source can be compressed to about its entropy but no further. And every noisy channel has a capacity: below it, suitable codes make errors as rare as you like without slowing the rate toward zero. He framed all communication the same way: source, encoder, noisy channel, decoder, destination. A fair coin toss carries exactly one bit; a coin that lands heads nine times in ten carries less, because its outcome is less surprising.
CS008.analogy: In the game of twenty questions, each well-chosen yes-or-no answer is one bit. Entropy is roughly how many questions you need on average to identify the message, and the channel capacity is how many questions’ worth of answers can get across despite a noisy phone line.
CS008.unlocked: Shannon’s theory underlies data compression (ZIP, JPEG, MP3), error-correcting codes (compact discs, deep-space links, Wi-Fi and mobile networks), and the whole idea of digital communication. It made the bit the unit of information and brought a statistical view of messages that spread to linguistics, biology, cryptography and machine learning. Chomsky’s study of language began by pushing against its statistical models of text.
CS008.left_open: Shannon proved that good codes exist without saying how to build practical ones. It took decades of work, from Hamming and Reed–Solomon to turbo and LDPC codes, to approach capacity. And his information is about symbols, not significance: the theory deliberately ignores what a message means, so it says nothing about meaning, relevance or understanding.
CS008.diagram_alt: A communication chain: source, encoder, noisy channel with a noise source feeding in, decoder, destination. Below, three notes: entropy H is the average information in bits, a source can be compressed to about H, and reliable communication is possible below channel capacity C.

CS009.problem: By 1950 digital computers existed, and people argued about whether machines could think. The arguments tended to dissolve into disagreements about the word “think,” on which nobody agreed. Turing wanted a question that could be tested rather than endlessly debated, and he wanted to show that the arguments against machine intelligence were weaker than they looked.
CS009.insight: Turing replaced “Can machines think?” with a game. An interrogator exchanges typed messages with two hidden players, one human and one machine, and must decide which is which. If the machine can fool the interrogator often enough, we have no good grounds to deny it intelligence. This “imitation game,” now called the Turing test, turns a philosophical question into an empirical one. He then worked through objections: theological, mathematical (citing Gödel), the claim that machines can only do what they are told, and more. And he sketched a route to success: not programming an adult mind but building a “child machine” and educating it, so that learning is central. He predicted that by about the year 2000 an average interrogator would have no more than a 70 per cent chance of identifying the machine after five minutes of questioning.
CS009.analogy: It is a blind taste test. Instead of arguing about whether a wine is “really” a Burgundy, you ask whether experts can tell it from one when they cannot see the label.
CS009.unlocked: The paper made machine intelligence a respectable research goal and gave the field a recognisable benchmark. Its objections section anticipated many later debates, such as Searle’s Chinese room, and its “child machine” passage is an early statement of machine learning. It also drew directly on his own universal machine: because a digital computer can imitate any other machine, a computer with the right program could in principle imitate a mind.
CS009.left_open: The test measures conversation, and arguably only imitation: a program tuned to fool judges can pass without understanding anything. The paper offered no concrete method for building such a machine and no organised research programme. That came a few years later, when a small group chose a name and an agenda for the new field. Critics also point out that the test rewards deception and conversational tricks, which is why later researchers have proposed harder, more specific benchmarks.
CS009.diagram_alt: An interrogator on the left sends typed questions to two hidden players, A and B, on the right, separated by a screen. One player is a human and one is a machine. The question is whether the interrogator can tell which is which.

CS010.problem: In the early 1950s, work related to machine intelligence was scattered across several fields: cybernetics, automata theory, information theory, neural networks, computer chess. It had no common name, no shared agenda and no community. Researchers in different fields rarely met, and each used different vocabulary for similar ideas. Nobody had yet said, in one place, what a unified effort would try to do. The organisers themselves came from these separate strands: Shannon had written on programming a computer to play chess, and Minsky had built a neural-network learning machine as a student.
CS010.insight: John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester and Claude Shannon wrote to the Rockefeller Foundation asking for support for a two-month summer study at Dartmouth College in 1956. The key sentence is a conjecture: every aspect of learning, or any other feature of intelligence, can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it. They listed topics to study, including programming languages, neuron nets, the size of computations, self-improvement, abstraction, and randomness and creativity. The proposal also gave the field its name: “artificial intelligence.”
CS010.analogy: It works like a founding charter. A scattered group of researchers with similar questions gets a name, a banner and a list of problems, the way naming a conference “genomics” could turn many separate labs into one field.
CS010.unlocked: Artificial intelligence became an academic field, with labs at MIT, Stanford and Carnegie Mellon and a stream of funding. The workshop itself featured Newell and Simon’s Logic Theorist, and McCarthy went on to create LISP as a language for the field’s symbolic programs. The conjecture set the agenda for decades of symbolic AI: represent knowledge explicitly, then search and reason over it. The name itself stuck, even though some of the participants disliked it.
CS010.left_open: The proposal assumed that a small group could make significant progress in a single summer, which was wildly optimistic. It set out topics but no method, and soon the field split between symbolic reasoning and neural networks. Repeated cycles of overpromising and disappointment, later called AI winters, followed. The conjecture itself remains unproven: nobody has shown that every aspect of intelligence can be so precisely described.

CS011.problem: Linguists mostly catalogued the forms of languages. Shannon’s information theory had suggested a different idea: treat language as a statistical source in which each word depends on the few words before it. But nobody had a mathematically precise way to ask what kind of machinery a grammar of English requires, or to compare the power of different ways of writing grammars.
CS011.insight: Noam Chomsky compared three ways of describing a language. In finite-state (Markov) models, the next word depends on a bounded past. In phrase-structure grammars, rewriting rules such as S → NP VP build sentences from nested phrases. Transformational grammars add rules that rearrange those phrase structures. He argued that finite-state models cannot generate English, because sentences nest dependencies, such as “if… then” inside “either… or,” and matching them needs unbounded memory of what is still open. Phrase-structure rules can express nesting. In 1959 he organised grammars into the hierarchy now taught in computer science, whose levels match types of machine, from finite automata up to Turing machines.
CS011.analogy: Think of checking parentheses. A machine that remembers only the last symbol cannot tell whether every opening bracket gets a matching closer. You need a stack of what is currently open, and that extra memory is what separates the levels of the hierarchy.
CS011.unlocked: Chomsky’s work founded formal language theory, linking grammars to automata and giving computer science the tools to describe programming languages precisely. Context-free grammars became the standard way to specify syntax, and parsers and compilers are built directly from them. It also reshaped linguistics and the early study of language by computer, and its machine-matched levels remain a staple of the first course in the theory of computation. Pushdown automata and regular expressions, tools programmers use daily, correspond to levels of this hierarchy.
CS011.left_open: Whether natural languages are really context-free, and how a child or a machine could learn a grammar from examples, stayed controversial. When speech recognition and machine translation finally succeeded in the 1980s and after, it was largely with statistical methods, the approach this paper had argued against. The neat generative picture and the data-driven one remained in tension.

CS012.problem: Programming early computers meant writing instructions one machine operation at a time, in numeric codes or assembly language. It was slow, error-prone and tied to one machine, and the cost of programming often rivalled the cost of the computer. Many experts believed an automatic translator from mathematical notation would produce code so slow that nobody would use it: machines were scarce and programmers took pride in hand-tuned code. Programmers also had to track where each number lived in memory, so rewriting a program for a new machine meant starting again.
CS012.insight: John Backus’s team at IBM designed a language in which scientists write formulas almost as they do in mathematics, with loops and conditions, and a compiler translates them into machine code. The real achievement was making the compiler good enough to win over sceptics. The team put much of their effort into optimisation, such as choosing registers wisely and avoiding repeated calculations, so the generated code ran nearly as fast as code written by hand. The system was delivered for the IBM 704 in 1957, after years of work.
CS012.analogy: It is like ordering a meal by naming the dish instead of describing each knife stroke to the cook. That only works if the cook is good enough that you do not miss your own instructions.
CS012.unlocked: FORTRAN proved that high-level languages could be efficient, which made them the default. It launched compiler construction as a discipline, with parsing, optimisation and code generation. Scientists and engineers could now write their own programs, and the language is still used today in scientific computing, such as weather and climate models and physics simulations. Every later language had to answer the question FORTRAN settled: it is possible to be both convenient and fast.
CS012.left_open: FORTRAN’s design was shaped by one machine and by numerical work. It had awkward control structures, leaning on GOTO, and at first no recursion and few ways to organise data beyond arrays. It was also hard to describe formally. Languages with cleaner structure came next, along with Dijkstra’s 1968 case against GOTO, and McCarthy’s LISP took programming in a quite different direction.

CS013.problem: Given a map of towns joined by roads of different lengths, how do you find the shortest route from one town to another? The obvious method is to check every possible route, but the number of routes explodes as the map grows, beyond what any computer could handle. A usable method needed effort that grows modestly with the size of the map, and a guarantee that its answer really is the shortest.
CS013.insight: Edsger Dijkstra’s method keeps a set of towns whose shortest distance from the start is already known. Repeatedly it takes the nearest town not yet settled and fixes its distance, because no route through any other unsettled town could be shorter, since road lengths are never negative. Then it updates the distance estimates of that town’s neighbours. Each step settles exactly one town, so the work grows roughly with the square of the number of towns instead of exploding. The paper is three pages long; the heart of it is the argument for why the greedy choice is safe, a proof of correctness as much as a procedure. It also gave a method for the cheapest way of connecting all the towns.
CS013.analogy: Think of ripples spreading from a stone dropped in a pond. The water reaches the nearest points first, and once the ripple touches a point you know that is the earliest it can arrive.
CS013.unlocked: Dijkstra’s algorithm became a staple: it sits inside internet routing protocols such as OSPF, in map and navigation software, and in countless planning and optimisation tools. More broadly it showed the style of algorithm design where a clever invariant lets a locally best choice be globally right. Dijkstra himself carried that emphasis on proving correctness into his later work on programming.
CS013.left_open: The method fails if road lengths can be negative, which later algorithms such as Bellman–Ford handle. Its roughly quadratic cost was fine for small maps but not for very large sparse ones, until better data structures reduced it. And the paper had no general way to compare algorithms or say what is fundamentally hard: that needed a theory of computational complexity, which began in the following decade.
CS013.diagram_alt: A small road map with towns S, A, B, C and T and numbered road lengths. Distances settle in the order S 0, B 2, A 3, C 8, T 11, and the shortest route S, B, A, C, T of length 11 is highlighted.
review: OSPF uses shortest-path-first (Dijkstra) computation
E026 (CS013 to CS020) is interpretive: a reading that Dijkstra's cost accounting foreshadows complexity theory
The paper solves two problems: the shortest path and the minimum spanning tree

CS014.problem: Artificial intelligence research needed programs that manipulate symbols and structures, such as logical formulas, sentences and plans, not just numbers. FORTRAN was built for arithmetic. It had no recursion at first, no easy way to build structures while running, and no way for a program to treat another program as data. Programmers also lacked a clean mathematical account of what a program means. Researchers building the first AI programs were writing them in assembly code or in IPL, a list-processing language that was powerful but low-level.
CS014.insight: John McCarthy defined a tiny language. Data are symbolic expressions: atoms and pairs, which chain into lists. Programs are written as the same kind of expression. A handful of primitive operations (car, cdr, cons, atom, eq), conditional expressions, function definitions using Church’s lambda notation, and recursion are enough to build the rest. He then wrote the language’s own interpreter in the language itself, a function now called eval, a few lines that can run any program given as a list. It is the programming-language counterpart of Turing’s universal machine. To manage memory in a world of freely built lists, the design also introduced automatic garbage collection.
CS014.analogy: Imagine a recipe book whose recipes are written so uniformly that one chapter can teach the cook to read every other chapter, including itself.
CS014.unlocked: LISP became the main language of symbolic AI for three decades, and its ideas spread everywhere: recursion, conditionals as expressions, functions as values, garbage collection, interactive read-eval-print loops and code that writes code. Later dialects such as Scheme became the teaching language of Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs, and today’s lambda expressions and metaprogramming in mainstream languages trace back to it. The notation also made it natural to write programs that take programs as input, and symbolic differentiation was one of the first applications.
CS014.left_open: Early LISP was slow and hungry for memory, and ran best on specialised machines. Its original scoping rules caused subtle bugs, and its uniform parenthesised syntax was hard on human readers. The deeper question it served, whether manipulating symbols is enough to produce intelligence, remained open and would divide AI into rival camps.
CS014.diagram_alt: The list (A (B C)) drawn as linked pairs of cells, beside the program (+ 1 (* 2 3)) written as the same kind of list, and an eval box that takes any such list and runs it, showing that code and data share one structure.
review: McCarthy 1960 cites Church's lambda notation (basis for E022 explicit)
E023: McCarthy draws the analogy of eval to a universal machine; tagged interpretive until the 1960 text is checked
Garbage collection was introduced in the LISP design (described in the 1960 paper)
Seven-primitive list: car, cdr, cons, atom, eq plus conditionals and lambda; check the exact primitive set against the paper

CS015.problem: In the early 1960s computers were seen mainly as fast calculators and as machines for automating clerical work. Meanwhile the problems that mattered, in science, engineering, government and business, were growing more complex than any one mind could hold. Douglas Engelbart asked a different question: not how to make computers do people’s work, but how to make people more capable at their own. At the time there was no framework for thinking about that, no vocabulary for what a computer might do to improve human thinking itself, and almost no machine that a person could use interactively.
CS015.insight: Engelbart defined “augmenting human intellect” as increasing a person’s capability to approach a complex problem, to gain comprehension suited to their needs, and to find solutions. His key move was to treat the human as one part of a system with four parts: Humans using Language, Artifacts, Methodology and Training, abbreviated H-LAM/T. Improving any one part, or the way they fit together, improves the whole. Computers belonged in this picture as artifacts that could store, rearrange and link symbols as quickly as ideas change, and so could change the language and methods people use to think. The paper works through a scenario of a person at work with such a machine, drafting, restructuring and cross-referencing ideas, in which the working process itself is transformed.
CS015.analogy: Think of the difference between a pocket calculator and a pencil that remembers, links and rearranges everything you have ever written. The first replaces a task; the second changes how you think and how far you can see.
CS015.unlocked: Engelbart went on to build his ideas at the Stanford Research Institute. In 1968 his team gave a public demonstration, later nicknamed “the mother of all demos,” showing a mouse, windows, hyperlinked text, shared-screen collaboration and video conferencing on one system. Many of these ideas reached personal computing through researchers who moved on to Xerox PARC, and from there to graphical interfaces, word processors and the links between documents on the web. Beyond the particular tools, the paper changed the goal of interactive computing: from automating people to amplifying them.
CS015.left_open: The paper is a framework, not a working system, and it assumed computing power that was scarce and shared. Engelbart accepted that powerful tools could take real effort to learn, a choice that later designers, aiming at ease of use for everyone, would question. His vision centred on skilled groups solving hard problems, and left open how such tools would reach ordinary people, what they would cost, and how anyone could measure whether a person had really been augmented.
CS015.diagram_alt: A person at the centre, augmented by four surrounding parts: language (ways of expressing ideas), artifacts (tools, now computers), methodology (ways of working) and training (skills to use them). Improving any part, or how they fit, improves the whole.
review: Engelbart 1962 cites Vannevar Bush's As We May Think (basis for ghost G006 and edge E029, tagged explicit)
1968 demonstration showed mouse, windows, hypertext, shared-screen collaboration and video conferencing
E031 and E032 (Engelbart to Smalltalk and to the Web proposal) are interpretive readings of influence

CS016.problem: Sorting is one of the most common jobs a computer does, and in 1960 it was expensive. Memories were small, and the standard methods were either simple but slow, taking time that grows with the square of the number of items, or fast but needing a second copy of the data in a memory that could barely hold the first. Hoare met the problem while working on machine translation, where a dictionary of words had to be kept in order. He needed a method that was fast on average and could sort in place.
CS016.insight: Quicksort works by choosing one item, the pivot, and rearranging the others so that everything smaller comes before it and everything larger comes after. The pivot is then in its final place. The two groups on either side are sorted the same way, by applying the same method to each. Because each step splits the problem into smaller pieces, the typical amount of work grows only a little faster than the number of items, in proportion to n log n, and the rearranging happens inside the original array with very little extra memory. Hoare stated the method as a recursive procedure in ALGOL, a language whose support for recursion let the idea be written in a few lines.
CS016.analogy: To sort a pile of exam papers, pick one paper, put the lower marks in one pile and the higher in another, then do the same to each pile. Nobody ever has to compare papers across piles again.
CS016.unlocked: Quicksort became the workhorse of general-purpose sorting. Versions of it sit behind the sort routines in standard libraries, and it is often the first example taught of divide and conquer, in which a problem is split into smaller copies of itself. It also pushed the study of average-case analysis and of randomised algorithms: choosing the pivot at random makes a bad case unlikely whatever the input. And it showed that recursion, once thought a curiosity, was a practical tool for algorithm design, which helped carry recursion into mainstream programming languages.
CS016.left_open: In the worst case, for example when the input is already sorted and the pivot is always the first item, Quicksort takes time proportional to the square of the number of items. Good pivot choice, such as taking the median of three items or choosing at random, makes this rare but not impossible, and later hybrids such as introsort add a safety net. Quicksort is also not stable, meaning that equal items may change their order, which matters when sorting by several keys one after another.
CS016.diagram_alt: A row of eight numbers is partitioned around the pivot 5 into the smaller items 2, 1, 3, 4 on the left and the larger items 8, 9, 7 on the right; each side is then sorted the same way.
review: Hoare invented Quicksort while working on machine translation in Moscow (his own recollection)
The 1962 paper presents the algorithm in ALGOL 60 (basis for ghost G007 and edge E033, tagged explicit)
Introsort (Musser, 1997) is the usual hybrid that guards against the worst case

CS017.problem: In 1962 using a computer meant preparing a deck of punched cards or typing coded commands, then waiting for printed output. Pictures were hard: a drawing had to be described in numbers, one coordinate at a time. Engineers and designers thought in diagrams, and there was no way to sketch a figure on a computer, adjust it, and see the machine respond. The question Ivan Sutherland took up in his MIT doctoral thesis was whether a person and a computer could hold a conversation through pictures.
CS017.insight: Sketchpad ran on the experimental TX-2 computer, with a cathode-ray display and a light pen the user pointed at the screen. You drew lines, circles and arcs directly. What made it more than a drawing tool was that shapes carried rules. You could state that two lines must be parallel, that a corner must be a right angle, or that a segment has a fixed length, and Sketchpad would solve for positions that satisfied all of the constraints at once, moving the rest of the drawing as you pulled on one part. It also separated a master drawing from its instances: change the master, say a rivet or a symbol, and every copy changed, and copies could be scaled and rotated.
CS017.analogy: It is a drafting table where the lines remember what they are meant to be. Push one corner of a parallelogram and the rest keeps its shape, because the sketch knows the rules, not just the ink.
CS017.unlocked: Sketchpad founded interactive computer graphics and computer-aided design, and is the ancestor of drawing programs. Pointing at things on a screen to act on them, now called direct manipulation, became the model for graphical interfaces. The master-and-instance idea anticipated object-oriented programming, and Alan Kay has said that it influenced his thinking about Smalltalk. Its constraint solving seeded a line of work on constraint-based design tools that still shapes how design software keeps drawings consistent.
CS017.left_open: Sketchpad needed a room-sized research computer, so it was a demonstration rather than a product. It worked in two dimensions, and its solving method was slow and could fail to converge on awkward constraints. Making this style of interaction cheap enough for ordinary users depended on hardware, such as low-cost displays and graphics processors, that did not yet exist, and on interface ideas such as the mouse and windows that came later.
CS017.diagram_alt: A screen showing a parallelogram with marks for parallel sides and equal lengths, and a light pen touching one corner. Beside it, a master drawing with three scaled copies, its instances, that change whenever the master changes.
review: Sutherland's thesis was done at MIT on the TX-2 with a light pen
Alan Kay has credited Sketchpad as an influence on Smalltalk and object-oriented ideas (basis for E035, tagged interpretive)
E030 (Engelbart to Sketchpad) is an interpretive reading: both treat the computer as an interactive partner in thinking

CS018.problem: Many signals, such as sound, radio, seismic vibrations and images, are easier to understand as a mix of frequencies than as a series of raw measurements. The discrete Fourier transform turns one view into the other. But computing it directly for n measurements takes about n times n operations. A thousand samples means a million steps; a million samples means a trillion. In the early 1960s, when scientists wanted to analyse seismic records, for example to tell nuclear tests from earthquakes, the direct method was too slow to be practical.
CS018.insight: James Cooley and John Tukey showed how to split the work. Suppose the number of samples can be divided into smaller factors, say n = 2 × (n/2). The transform of the whole series can be built from two transforms of half the size, one on the even-numbered samples and one on the odd-numbered, combined with a few multiplications by roots of unity. Those smaller transforms can be split again, and again, until only trivial ones remain. The repeated halving brings the cost down from about n² to about n log n: for a million samples, around twenty million operations rather than a trillion. The same idea had been found before, even by Gauss around 1805, but it went unpublished or unnoticed; the 1965 paper made it known at the moment computers could use it.
CS018.analogy: Instead of comparing every contestant against every other, a knockout tournament pairs up small groups and reuses their results. The FFT gets its speed in the same way: it reuses partial answers instead of recomputing them.
CS018.unlocked: The FFT made digital signal processing practical. It sits inside audio and image compression, radio and Wi-Fi and mobile networks, radar and sonar, medical imaging such as MRI, and the numerical solution of equations. It also gives a fast way to multiply very large numbers and to compute convolutions, which later mattered for neural networks. It is often cited as one of the most influential algorithms of the twentieth century, and as the standard example of a smarter algorithm beating faster hardware.
CS018.left_open: The original method worked best when the number of samples was a power of two, and later work extended it to other sizes. It deals with idealised numbers; real implementations must manage rounding errors and the way data moves through memory, which on modern machines often costs more than the arithmetic. And it applies to regular, evenly spaced samples; signals measured at irregular times need other methods.
CS018.diagram_alt: A transform of n points is split into two transforms of n/2 points, on the even and odd samples, and split again. For n = 1,024 the direct method needs about 1,048,576 operations while the fast method needs about 10,240, roughly a hundred times fewer.
review: Gauss's unpublished use of the same idea around 1805 (rediscovered by Heideman, Johnson and Burrus, 1984)
Seismic test-ban monitoring as a motivating application (Tukey's account)
E036 (Shannon to FFT) and E037 (FFT to TAOCP) are interpretive; Knuth treats the FFT in later volumes, not Volume 1

CS019.problem: In 1965 the integrated circuit was only a few years old, and many in the electronics industry doubted it would ever be economical. Circuits made from separate components were cheap and well understood, while integrated ones were costly and new, with low yields. Engineers and managers had to decide whether to invest in a technology whose future was unclear, and no one had put a shape on how quickly it might improve.
CS019.insight: Gordon Moore, then at Fairchild Semiconductor, plotted the number of components that could be placed on a single chip at the lowest cost per component, year by year. The points fell on a straight line on a logarithmic scale: the number had been doubling about every year. He extrapolated ten years ahead, to roughly sixty-five thousand components on a chip by 1975, and argued that integration would make electronics cheaper, smaller and more reliable. In 1975 he revised the pace to a doubling about every two years. The word “law” came later, from others; it is a trend with economic reasons, not a law of physics.
CS019.analogy: It reads like a train timetable that the whole industry decided to keep. Because everyone planned products and factories around the next doubling, the forecast helped make itself come true.
CS019.unlocked: The curve became the industry’s planning rhythm. Chipmakers, equipment suppliers and designers lined up their roadmaps to it, and computers got faster and cheaper on a steady schedule for fifty years. Software developers could assume that tomorrow’s machine would be more capable, which shaped what they were willing to build. Cheap, dense chips made personal computers, phones and sensors everywhere possible, and the expectation of exponential progress spread to talk about other technologies.
CS019.left_open: A trend with no mechanism cannot last forever. Transistors approach the size of a few atoms, and once power per unit area stopped falling in the mid-2000s, clock speeds levelled off and designers turned to multiple cores, which bring the limits that Amdahl described. Chip factories have become enormously expensive. The paper forecasts but does not explain, and says little about whether more components make better systems or what to do with them.
CS019.diagram_alt: A chart on a logarithmic scale of components per chip against year: a rising line from 1959 to 1965, then a dashed extrapolation reaching about 65,000 components by 1975, a doubling every year.
review: The 1965 forecast was a doubling every year; Moore revised it to every two years in 1975
Dennard scaling ended in the mid-2000s, after which clock speeds flattened and multicore followed
The curve in the diagram is schematic (a doubling each year), not Moore's exact plotted points
Ghost G008 is titled 'Transistor and integrated circuit' (1947); E038 is interpretive because Moore does not cite the inventors

CS020.problem: By the early 1960s the theory of computation, begun by Turing and Church, could say which problems no machine can solve. It said nothing about how hard the solvable ones are. A problem that takes a billion years on any computer is solvable only in name, and programmers were already finding that some problems were far more costly than others. What was missing was a precise way to measure the resources a computation uses and to compare problems by their cost.
CS020.insight: Juris Hartmanis and Richard Stearns, working at General Electric’s research laboratory, measured cost as the number of steps a Turing machine takes, as a function of the size of the input. They grouped problems by how fast the best machine can solve them: those solvable in a number of steps proportional to n, those in n squared, and so on. Their central theorem shows that these groups are genuinely different: give a machine enough extra time and it can solve problems that no machine with less time can. Time is not just a nuisance; more of it buys more power. The paper also fixed the vocabulary, and gave the field its name, computational complexity.
CS020.analogy: Computability asks whether a road exists between two cities. Complexity asks how long the drive takes as the map grows, and whether a faster route could ever exist.
CS020.unlocked: This is the start of computational complexity theory. It led directly to the study of polynomial time, to Cook’s and Karp’s work on NP-completeness, and to the P versus NP question that remains the best-known open problem in computer science. For practice, it gave algorithm designers a shared yardstick: describing an algorithm by how its cost grows with input size, rather than by timings on one machine. Hartmanis and Stearns received the Turing Award in 1993 for founding the field.
CS020.left_open: The paper’s hierarchy shows that more time buys more power, but says little about problems people actually care about, such as scheduling or routing. It also depends on the machine model: step counts change with the kind of Turing machine, and later work had to ask which classes survive such changes. Proving that a specific natural problem needs a lot of time turned out to be extremely hard, and still is.
CS020.diagram_alt: Nested classes of problems solvable in time n, then n squared, then 2 to the n, each strictly containing the last, beside curves showing how steps grow with input size for the three cases.
review: Hartmanis and Stearns were at General Electric Research Laboratory; Turing Award 1993
Their hierarchy theorem: given sufficiently more time, strictly more can be computed
E040 (to Cook) is interpretive: Cook's framework is polynomial time on Turing machines; check whether Cook cites Hartmanis and Stearns directly

CS021.problem: In the mid-1960s designers of the fastest computers were tempted by a new idea: instead of making one processor faster, connect many and let them work at once. The arithmetic looked simple: ten processors, ten times the speed. Companies and governments were preparing to spend large sums on that bet. Gene Amdahl, who had designed IBM’s mainframes, doubted that it would pay off for real work, but there was no clear way to say how much parallel machines could actually gain.
CS021.insight: Amdahl’s short argument, presented at a 1967 conference, was that real programs contain a stubborn fraction that must be done in order, such as managing data, deciding what to do next, and combining results. Parallel processors can speed up only the rest. If a tenth of a job is sequential, even infinitely many processors can never make it more than ten times faster. The compact formula, speedup = 1 / ((1 − p) + p / n) for a parallel fraction p on n processors, was derived later from his argument. With 95 per cent of a task parallel, a thousand processors give less than twenty times the speed. His conclusion: effort spent on parallelism is wasted unless sequential speed improves as well.
CS021.analogy: A restaurant can hire more cooks, but a roast still takes three hours in the oven. However many cooks you add, the meal cannot arrive before the roast does.
CS021.unlocked: Amdahl’s law became the basic tool for reasoning about speedup, and it generalises to any improvement: the gain is limited by the share of time that the improved part accounts for. It shaped how architects choose what to optimise, made the sequential fraction a first-class concern for parallel programmers, and became a standard topic in textbooks. When multicore chips arrived in the 2000s, it explained why adding cores often disappointed. It also provoked the counter-argument, from John Gustafson in 1988, that larger machines are used to solve bigger problems.
CS021.left_open: The argument assumes the problem size is fixed, which is why it is pessimistic: with bigger machines people run bigger jobs, where the sequential fraction can shrink. It treats the sequential fraction as given, though a better algorithm can sometimes reduce it. And it ignores the costs of communication and coordination between processors, which in practice often limit speedup earlier than the serial fraction does.
CS021.diagram_alt: A chart of speedup against number of processors on a logarithmic axis. Curves for tasks that are 50, 90 and 95 per cent parallel flatten out at speedups of 2, 10 and 20 however many processors are added.
review: The 1967 paper states the argument in words; the speedup formula was derived afterwards by others
Amdahl's 1967 sentence: parallel effort is wasted unless accompanied by sequential improvements of the same magnitude
Gustafson's law (1988) is the standard counter-argument
E042 (to Hennessy and Patterson) is tagged explicit: they present Amdahl's law as a central principle

CS022.problem: By the late 1960s programs had grown to thousands of lines, and many were written as tangles of jumps. The goto statement, which sends execution to any labelled point, was a standard tool, and in languages such as FORTRAN it was almost unavoidable. Programmers found these programs hard to understand and harder to get right, but no one had a convincing account of why. The difficulty is that a person reads a program as static text, from top to bottom, while what matters is what happens as the program runs.
CS022.insight: Dijkstra’s answer, in a two-page letter to Communications of the ACM, was that people are poor at following processes in time, so a program’s text should mirror its run as closely as possible. To pin down a point in a running program you need only a few coordinates when the code is built from sequences, choices (if) and repetitions (loops, procedure calls): where you are in the text, and how many times round each loop. Unrestricted jumps destroy this: the number of coordinates needed explodes, and you can no longer tell the state of the program from where it is. He concluded that the quality of programmers falls as the density of gotos in their programs rises, and that the construct should be abolished from higher-level languages. The editor, Niklaus Wirth, gave the letter its famous title.
CS022.analogy: Following a route described as “turn left, then right, then straight on” is easy. Following one that says “go to instruction 47” on every line, where instruction 47 says “go back to instruction 12,” is not, because you can never tell how you arrived.
CS022.unlocked: The letter launched the structured programming movement. Languages after ALGOL 60 and FORTRAN, from Pascal to C and its descendants, were designed around blocks, conditionals and loops, and the idea that code should be readable from top to bottom became a basic norm. It also linked directly to proving programs correct, since structured pieces can be reasoned about one at a time, as Hoare’s axioms did the next year. And its title started the habit of publishing “considered harmful” essays.
CS022.left_open: Dijkstra offered argument, not evidence, and goto does have uses. Donald Knuth argued in 1974 for a balanced view, noting that jumping out of a loop or handling an error can be clearer with a goto. Languages later added structured ways to do these things, such as break statements and exceptions, which bring back some of the jumping the letter feared. What exactly makes a program’s structure understandable remained a research question, with later answers in modularity and abstraction.
CS022.diagram_alt: On the left, six numbered statements joined by crossing jump arrows, hard to follow. On the right, three structured building blocks: sequence, choice and repetition, which keep the order of the text close to the order of execution.
review: Wirth, as editor, retitled Dijkstra's letter 'Go To Statement Considered Harmful' (Dijkstra's original title was 'A case against the goto statement')
The quoted claim about programmer quality and goto density is paraphrased from the letter
Knuth's 1974 paper 'Structured Programming with go to Statements' argues for a balanced view
E043 and E044 are interpretive: they read FORTRAN as the practice and ALGOL 60 as the structured alternative

CS023.problem: By the mid-1960s computers were fast and getting cheaper, but the programs for them were not keeping pace. Big projects, such as IBM’s OS/360 operating system, ran years late, cost far more than planned and shipped with errors. Many people felt something was fundamentally wrong with how software was produced, but it was seen as a collection of local failures in individual projects rather than as a shared problem with a name and a field to study it.
CS023.insight: In October 1968 the NATO Science Committee brought about fifty people from industry, universities and government to Garmisch, Germany, to discuss what its organisers provocatively called “software engineering.” The aim of the name was to suggest that software should be made with the same discipline as bridges or aircraft: planned, specified, designed with defined methods, tested and maintained. The participants described a “software crisis” and recorded their talk and disagreements in a report edited by Peter Naur and Brian Randell. Sessions covered design, production, service and the relation between hardware and software; Douglas McIlroy argued for mass-produced, reusable software components. The report is unusual in recording the discussion itself, including doubts, as a kind of conversation.
CS023.analogy: It is the moment a trade names itself. Before “civil engineering” there were builders whose bridges sometimes fell down; the name carried the promise of method, standards and a body of knowledge.
CS023.unlocked: The conference gave the field its name and its agenda: methods of design, specification, testing and project management, and the idea that software development needs a lifecycle and professional standards. University degrees, journals and standards bodies followed. It set the context for the 1970s work on modular design by Parnas and the management lessons of Brooks, and for the structured programming movement; a follow-up conference in Rome in 1969 continued the discussion. And it popularised the phrase “software crisis,” which framed the next decades.
CS023.left_open: The engineering analogy has always been contested: software is not manufactured, has no physical constraints to guide it, and every project is largely design. The “crisis” turned out to be chronic; two decades on, Brooks would argue that no single technique could end it. The report records problems and opinions, not solutions, and the debate between treating programming as a craft, a science or engineering, and between heavyweight planning and lightweight agility, is still going.
CS023.diagram_alt: A box listing the symptoms of the software crisis: late, over budget, unreliable and hard to maintain, with an arrow to a box listing what a software engineering discipline would provide: design methods, production control, testing and quality, and maintenance. Garmisch, Germany, October 1968.
review: Conference at Garmisch, Germany, October 1968, sponsored by the NATO Science Committee; report edited by Naur and Randell
'About fifty people' attended: verify the count and the number of countries
McIlroy's 'Mass produced software components' was presented at Garmisch
A second NATO conference followed in Rome in 1969
E052 and E053 (to Parnas and to Brooks) are interpretive

CS024.problem: By the mid-1960s computer programming had grown into a huge body of techniques, but the knowledge was scattered across journal articles, manuals and the heads of practitioners. Much of it was tied to particular machines, and there was no standard of careful analysis: an algorithm was judged by whether it seemed to work and ran fast enough on someone’s computer. Programmers lacked a single, mathematically sound and practical reference for what was known and how to compare methods.
CS024.insight: Donald Knuth began, as a young professor, an ambitious plan for a comprehensive treatise on algorithms, in several volumes. Volume 1, Fundamental Algorithms, covered basic concepts, including what an algorithm is and the mathematics needed to study one, and the information structures, such as lists, stacks, queues and trees, on which other methods build. Its distinctive choices were to treat each method with mathematical rigour, to analyse how many operations it takes rather than just describing it, and to give concrete programs in the assembly language of MIX, an invented computer, so that costs could be counted exactly without depending on a real machine. It gathered history, exercises with answers and references alongside the results.
CS024.analogy: Think of a cookbook that also explains the chemistry of each dish and tells you exactly how many minutes each step costs, with a history of every recipe and exercises to try it yourself.
CS024.unlocked: The series became the standard reference for algorithms and helped create analysis of algorithms as a field: asking not only whether a method works but exactly how its cost behaves. Its style of exposition influenced generations of textbooks. Knuth received the Turing Award in 1974, citing this work. Disappointment with the typesetting of the second edition led him to create the TeX typesetting system and the idea of literate programming, which in turn shaped how scientific text and code are written.
CS024.left_open: The work is vast and unfinished: later volumes covering seminumerical algorithms, sorting and searching, combinatorial algorithms and more have appeared over decades, with others still planned. The hypothetical MIX machine, even after its replacement by a more modern design, is far from today’s hardware, where caches and parallelism often matter more than operation counts. The treatment is demanding for beginners, and it predates topics such as object-oriented design, concurrency and the web that came to dominate programming.
CS024.diagram_alt: Five volumes of The Art of Computer Programming shown as books: Fundamental Algorithms (1968, highlighted), Seminumerical Algorithms (1969), Sorting and Searching (1973), Combinatorial Algorithms (from 2011) and Syntactic Algorithms (planned). A note says Volume 1 introduces MIX, an imaginary computer, so costs can be counted exactly.
review: Volume dates: 1 (1968), 2 (1969), 3 (1973), 4A (2011); Volume 5 planned
Knuth received the 1974 Turing Award, citing TAOCP among other contributions
TeX was prompted by dissatisfaction with the typesetting of the second edition of Volume 2 (1977)
E034 and E037 (Quicksort and FFT into TAOCP) are interpretive: those algorithms are treated in later volumes

CS025.problem: By the mid-1960s operating systems were becoming the most complicated programs anyone had written, since they had to share one computer among many users and devices at once. Systems like these were routinely late and unreliable, and when they failed it was almost impossible to find out why, because everything interacted with everything else. Dijkstra and his group at the Eindhoven University of Technology (Technische Hogeschool Eindhoven, hence THE) set out to build a small multiprogramming system that could be understood and shown to work.
CS025.insight: They organised the system as a hierarchy of layers, each one built only on those below. The bottom layer hid the single processor and made it look like many, one per process; the next managed memory and a rotating drum used as backing store; above it came the console, the buffering of input and output, the user programs, and the operator. Because each layer saw the one below as a clean abstract machine, it could be designed and tested completely before the next was added, and errors were found in the layer where they arose. Concurrency was controlled with a new primitive, the semaphore, with its two operations, P and V, which let sequential processes wait for each other safely.
CS025.analogy: It is like a chain of offices in which each clerk deals only with the clerk directly below. You can check each clerk’s work on its own, and nobody needs to know how the floors below do their jobs.
CS025.unlocked: THE showed that an operating system could be designed systematically, with levels of abstraction that remain a core idea of software and hardware design. Semaphores became the basic tool for synchronisation, the ancestors of the locks and monitors used in concurrent programs today, and “cooperating sequential processes” became the standard way to think about concurrency. The paper’s influence on later systems, including UNIX, came through its way of thinking, structuring a large system as a hierarchy of simple parts, rather than through code.
CS025.left_open: Strict layering has costs: calls pass down through several layers, and some functions depend on each other in ways that resist a clean order. The system was small and ran on a single machine type; whether the method scales to huge, evolving systems was unproven. Semaphores are easy to use wrongly, leading to deadlock, and later designs such as Hoare’s monitors tried to make synchronisation safer. And the claim of correctness rested on careful testing and reasoning rather than a complete formal proof.
CS025.diagram_alt: Six layers of the THE system stacked from layer 0, processor allocation, up through memory, console messages, input and output buffering and user programs to layer 5, the operator. Each layer uses only the one below. A side box describes semaphores with wait and signal operations.
review: The six levels of THE: 0 processor allocation, 1 memory and drum, 2 console message interpreter, 3 I/O buffering, 4 user programs, 5 operator
Semaphores (P and V) are described in the THE paper and in Dijkstra's earlier notes on cooperating sequential processes
E054 (to UNIX) and E055 (to Lamport) are interpretive readings of influence

CS026.problem: Programs were checked by running them on sample inputs, but testing can show that bugs are present, never that they are absent. As programs controlled more important things, that was uncomfortable. Mathematicians prove theorems from axioms; could one prove that a program does what it should? Robert Floyd had shown how to attach assertions to flowcharts, but a method was needed that worked on the text of programs, in the structured form that Dijkstra and others were advocating.
CS026.insight: Hoare’s paper opens by claiming that computer programming is an exact science, in that all the properties of a program can in principle be found out from its text by purely deductive reasoning. Its tool is the triple {P} S {Q}: if the condition P holds before the statement S runs, and S finishes, then Q holds afterwards. He gave axioms and rules for each construct. For assignment, the condition after is obtained by substituting the assigned expression into it. Rules for sequencing, choice and loops let proofs of pieces be combined. For a loop, one finds an invariant, a statement that stays true each time round, and then reads off what holds when it ends. Programs and their proofs can then be built together.
CS026.analogy: It works like a contract. If you give me ingredients that meet these conditions, I promise a result that meets those, and the rules let you check that each step of the recipe keeps the promise.
CS026.unlocked: Hoare logic is the foundation of program verification. Dijkstra’s weakest preconditions, design by contract with its preconditions and postconditions, and verification tools such as Dafny, SPARK and Frama-C all build on its ideas, and loop invariants are taught in nearly every algorithms course. It also gave a precise way to write specifications, saying exactly what a piece of code promises. And it made correctness something a program’s author could design for, not merely test for.
CS026.left_open: Hand proofs are laborious, and the method was first shown for small programs. Pointers and shared data, procedures, and concurrency were hard to handle and needed later extensions. The rules prove “partial correctness”: if the program finishes, the answer is right, and termination needs a separate argument. Above all, a proof shows that a program meets its specification, not that the specification is what anyone wanted; and proofs of whole real systems remain exceptional.
CS026.diagram_alt: A Hoare triple: a precondition P, a program statement S and a postcondition Q, with the example that if x is greater than 0 before the statement y becomes x plus 1, then y is greater than 1 afterwards. The rules cover assignment, sequence, choice and loops with an invariant.
review: Hoare 1969 opens with the claim that programming is an exact science (paraphrased in the text)
Floyd's 1967 'Assigning meanings to programs' preceded Hoare's work

CS027.problem: In the late 1960s, companies stored their data in files and in database systems that organised it as trees or networks of records joined by pointers. Programs were written to follow those pointers step by step, so a program knew exactly how the data was laid out: in what order, under which index, along which path. When the layout changed, programs broke. And every new question needed a new program written by a specialist. Edgar Codd, a mathematician at IBM, saw that this tangle of programs and storage was holding back the people who used the data.
CS027.insight: Codd proposed describing data as relations: simple tables of rows in which every fact is a value, and connections between tables are made by matching values, not by following pointers. Users then state what they want, using a small set of operations from set theory and logic, such as selecting rows, choosing columns and joining tables, and the system works out how to get it. This separates the logical view of the data from how it is stored, which Codd called data independence. He also gave rules, now called normalisation, for arranging data so that each fact is stored once, and showed that the model’s query operations are grounded in mathematics, which allows them to be reasoned about and optimised.
CS027.analogy: Instead of giving a taxi driver turn-by-turn directions through every street, you name the destination and let the driver choose the route. The relational model lets you say what data you want and leaves the route to the system.
CS027.unlocked: The relational model became the foundation of the database industry. IBM’s System R, the Ingres project at Berkeley and then Oracle, DB2, PostgreSQL and MySQL implemented it, and SQL, the query language that grew out of it, is still the everyday way to ask questions of data. Codd received the Turing Award in 1981. Because queries were declarative and grounded in mathematics, they could be automatically optimised, and that opened the way to the next era of data systems.
CS027.left_open: Early sceptics doubted that a system choosing its own access paths could ever be as fast as carefully hand-built navigation, a worry that had to be answered by query optimisation. The pure model struggles with some kinds of data, such as ordered lists, deeply nested documents and graphs, and real systems added nulls, duplicates and ordering that the theory leaves out. Decades later, the need to scale across many machines led some to abandon the relational model for simpler stores.
CS027.diagram_alt: On the left, records linked by pointers that a program must follow step by step. On the right, two tables, employees and departments, matched on the department value, so the user states what is wanted and the system chooses the route.
review: Codd was at IBM Research (San Jose) when he wrote the 1970 paper; Turing Award 1981
SQL grew out of IBM's SEQUEL language for System R

CS028.problem: By 1970 computer scientists knew that some problems seemed to need far more time than others. Finding the shortest route is quick; deciding whether a set of logical conditions can all be satisfied, or fitting items into the fewest bins, seemed to take exponentially longer as the problem grew. Whether these hard-looking problems really needed exponential time, or whether nobody had been clever enough, was unknown. There was no way to compare them or to explain why so many had resisted attack.
CS028.insight: Stephen Cook studied the problem of deciding whether a logical formula can be made true by some assignment of true and false to its variables, now called satisfiability, or SAT. He defined a class of problems whose proposed solutions can be checked quickly, later called NP. Then he proved that SAT is as hard as any of them: any problem in the class can be converted, in polynomial time, into a question of whether some formula is satisfiable. So if SAT could be solved quickly, every problem in NP could be. SAT is “NP-complete,” and the technique of reducing one problem to another became the way to measure difficulty.
CS028.analogy: Think of a master key. If you could open one special lock quickly, you would be able to open every lock in a huge family, because each can be turned into that lock. So that one lock is as hard as the whole family.
CS028.unlocked: Cook’s theorem created the theory of NP-completeness and the question of whether P equals NP, which remains the best-known unsolved problem in computer science. It gave Karp a method to show that dozens of famous problems were equally hard, and soon thousands more. It also gave engineers a practical warning sign: if a problem is NP-complete, stop looking for a fast exact method and use approximations or special cases. Modern SAT solvers, which handle enormous real instances, are used in chip and software verification. Cook received the Turing Award in 1982.
CS028.left_open: Whether P equals NP is still unknown, so no one has proved that NP-complete problems truly need exponential time; the result shows only that they stand or fall together. The theory measures worst cases, and many NP-complete problems are easy on typical instances, as SAT solvers show. And some important problems, such as factoring large numbers, sit in a grey zone: neither known to be easy nor shown to be NP-complete.
CS028.diagram_alt: Many problems in the class NP each reduce, by a quick conversion, to the satisfiability problem SAT. So a fast method for SAT would give a fast method for all of them.
review: The name NP and the term NP-complete came into use after Cook's paper (Karp 1972); Cook's paper works with 'P-reducibility' and tautologies
Cook received the 1982 Turing Award
